title: Argosy Health - Escalation Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up on the Jan 28th outage. Discussed root cause (KV cache eviction + router config during rolling deploy), short-term mitigations (rate limit adjustments, KV prefix pinning), and longer-term reliability work (automatic canarying, better autoscale SLOs, expanded observability). Agreed on timeline for mitigation PRs and a targeted benchmark run.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-02-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood CSM), Daniel Park (Argosy CTO), Sara Kim (Argosy SRE), Luis Fernandez (Argosy DevOps)

Summary: Quick follow-up to the Jan 28 outage. High-level recap, then dive into mitigations and longer term fixes.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, we know this is a busy week, appreciate it. The goal for today is to walk through what we found from the initial RCA, confirm mitigations, and align next steps.
[00:28] Daniel Park: Thanks Maya. Appreciate the summary you sent earlier. We want to make sure this doesn't recur—it's impacting our care workflows.
[00:37] Diego Ramirez: Yep, quick recap from engineering, apologies for some of the earlier typos in the doc — some names got mangled. Root cause we believe was KV cache eviction triggered during a rolling deploy when the routing config changed; a combination of short TTLs on prefix-cache entries and aggressive pod scale-down during the deploy. The cache misses amplified load to the primary model, which exposed a hot-path in the serving runtime.
[01:05] Sara Kim: Can you explain the serving runtime hot-path a bit — is it model decode or the attention kernel?
[01:12] Diego Ramirez: Good question. It was less about decode and more around KV cache rebuild costs + a fallback route that routed some traffic to a larger model variant unintentionally. The kernel selection ended up running an expensive path because sequence lengths spiked when certain prefixes were recomputed. There was also a routing rule that had a typo — we parsed it as a higher priority rule and it sent traffic to dedicated nodes that were momentarily constrained.
[01:46] Luis Fernandez: So this was both a config issue and resource contention, got it. We saw a lot of pod churn in our cluster metrics.
[01:54] Diego Ramirez: Exactly. Pod churn + KV eviction = cascade. For short term we recommend three mitigations: 1) pin critical prefixes in KV cache with longer TTLs, 2) adjust the rolling deploy policy to keep N extra pods for 5 minutes during deploys, 3) add a routing fallback to hosted model variant instead of the larger on-prem variant if capacity low.
[02:20] Maya Chen: To add, we'll also provide a quick patch to the routing config that removes that higher-priority typo rule and replace it with a canary flag so you can test without full traffic shift.
[02:35] Daniel Park: That sounds reasonable. Any security implications? We run in a VPC with KMS—will these changes affect encryption or audit logs?
[02:44] Priya Patel: Short answer: No for encryption keys, the KMS integration stays the same. Audit logs will still capture the deploy events and routing changes; we'll make sure the fix includes explicit audit annotations so your compliance team can trace the change. We'll attach SOC 2 notes.
[03:02] Sara Kim: We need the audit annotations since we have quarterly audits. Please include SSO/SAML user IDs in the change record.
[03:09] Maya Chen: Absolutely, we'll include the user IDs and the PR link in the audit entry.
[03:17] Diego Ramirez: A couple of notes about the KV cache benchmark we're proposing: we'll replay a sampled traffic trace from Jan 28 to emulate prefix distributions and burstiness. It's important we match your real sequence length distribution because quantization/attention kernel choices depend on that.
[03:36] Luis Fernandez: How invasive is the replay? We don't want production flakiness.
[03:40] Diego Ramirez: It will be against a shadow endpoint in your staging cluster or a sandbox we can spin up; we'll coordinate so it's off-peak. We'll share the script and the exact resource footprint beforehand.
[03:52] Daniel Park: Timeline?
[03:55] Diego Ramirez: We can run initial benchmarks within a week if you provide the traffic sample and cluster creds for the sandbox. Expect a 2-3 day run and then a results doc.
[04:06] Maya Chen: For the longer term, we proposed three reliability improvements in the doc: automatic canarying for config changes, improved autoscale SLOs with buffer capacity, and improved prefix-aware caching logic in the runtime to avoid full rebuilds.
[04:24] Sara Kim: Auto canarying—does Redwood provide that out of the box or is that a config pattern we implement?
[04:30] Diego Ramirez: We have canary tooling in the platform—it's not fully automated for every config type yet, but we can enable canary routes for routing and model selection policies. We also have a rollout policy that supports progressive traffic shifts with automatic rollback on error or latency SLO violations.
[04:49] Daniel Park: Would that help us avoid the need to have two model variants? We want cost controls.
[04:55] Maya Chen: Canarying would reduce blast radius, but for cost you can keep hosted fallback as a cheaper option. We discussed earlier switching to a lower-cost hosted model variant on overflow rather than a larger dedicated one. That reduces unit cost during incidents.
[05:09] Luis Fernandez: Any changes to billing or quotas if we route to hosted temporarily?
[05:13] Priya Patel: We'll make the billing implications explicit in the mitigation plan. Short-term surge will show up on usage; we can propose a temporary quota bump or a whitelisted emergency allowance so procurement isn't blocked.
[05:25] Daniel Park: Procurement will want that in writing.
[05:27] Maya Chen: We'll include a short addendum in the PR that calls out cost delta estimates for a 1-hour surge and for a sustained 24-hour reroute.
[05:37] Sara Kim: Back to root cause — you mentioned sequence length spikes. Could quantization or kernel change reduce the spike impact?
[05:44] Diego Ramirez: Potentially. Quantization helps throughput and memory, but the rebuild cost is still mostly a function of KV miss rate. If we can reduce misses via prefix pinning and better caching policy, quantization becomes a complementary win. Also the runtime's kernel selection can be tuned for expected sequence lengths — we'll include a recommended kernel profile.
[06:05] Daniel Park: Ok. On the action items, we need the logs and RCA. Maya, when can we get those?
[06:10] Maya Chen: I can send the initial logs and the RCA draft by EOD 2027-02-04. Diego will attach the benchmark plan and scripts.
[06:18] Diego Ramirez: I'll start on the replay script today and will need the traffic sample. If you can share that by 2027-02-05 we'll be on track to share results by 2027-02-09.
[06:29] Luis Fernandez: I'll extract the traffic sample and share. Also, we want the maintenance window to be late-night PST. Priya, can you coordinate with scheduling?
[06:36] Priya Patel: Yes, I'll propose two windows for 2027-02-12 and 2027-02-13 and capture your preferred hours.
[06:43] Daniel Park: On compliance again, please include the SOC 2 notes and explicit audit event IDs.
[06:49] Maya Chen: Will do. We'll attach the SOC 2 summary and map the changes to your audit framework.
[06:55] Sara Kim: One question — do you recommend Dedicated or staying Hosted + Dedicated fallback? We were evaluating Dedicated to reduce variability.
[07:03] Diego Ramirez: Dedicated gives you more predictable throughput, but it doesn't eliminate operator config errors. The hybrid approach (Dedicated primary + hosted fallback + strict autoscale buffers) gives both predictability and graceful degradation. If you want absolute isolation, Dedicated with stricter release controls and canarying is the way.
[07:23] Daniel Park: We'll review the cost tradeoffs but leaning hybrid for now.
[07:28] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick recap of next steps: Maya sends logs/RCA by 2027-02-04; Diego runs benchmark aiming for results by 2027-02-09; Priya schedules maintenance window by 2027-02-06; follow-up call on 2027-02-11.
[07:44] Luis Fernandez: Sounds good. Anything else?
[07:47] Daniel Park: No, thanks everyone. Appreciate the quick turnaround.
[07:50] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with the PR and docs.

End of meeting.
